text: Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister named Tamar, and David's son Amnon fell in love with her.
Amnon was so tormented over his sister Tamar that he made himself sick, since she was a virgin and it seemed impossible for him to get anywhere near her.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, son of David's brother Shimeah, and Jonadab was a very shrewd man.
Jonadab asked him why he, a king's son, looked so run-down morning after morning; Amnon admitted he was in love with Tamar, his brother Absalom's sister.
Jonadab told him to go to bed and act sick, and when his father came to check on him, to ask that Tamar be sent to fix food where he could watch and eat from her own hand.
So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill; when the king came to see him, Amnon asked that his sister Tamar be allowed to come make a couple of cakes in front of him so he could eat from her hand.
David sent orders to Tamar at the palace: go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him.
Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he lay in bed; she took dough, kneaded it, shaped cakes in his sight, and baked them.
She took the pan and served them out in front of him, but he refused to eat and told everyone to clear out, so they all left the room.
Then Amnon told Tamar to bring the food into the bedroom so he could eat from her hand; she carried the cakes she had made in to Amnon in the bedroom.
When she held them out for him to eat, he grabbed her and said, "Come sleep with me, my sister."
She said, "No, brother, don't force me — this kind of thing is not done in Israel. Don't do something so shameful."
"Where would I carry my disgrace? And you'd be branded like one of the shameless fools of Israel. Please, just speak to the king — he won't refuse to let you have me."
But he wouldn't listen to her, and since he was stronger, he overpowered her and raped her.
Then Amnon's feelings turned to hatred, a hatred even greater than the love he'd felt before, and he told her, "Get up and get out."
She answered, "No — sending me away now would be a worse wrong than what you already did to me." But he refused to listen.
He called the servant who attended him and said, "Get this woman out of here and bar the door after her."
She was wearing the long, ornamented robe unmarried royal daughters wore; the servant put her out and barred the door behind her.
Tamar put ashes on her head, tore the robe she had on, put her hand to her head, and went away wailing as she walked.
Her brother Absalom asked her, "Has Amnon been with you? For now, sister, stay quiet — he is your brother, don't let this consume you." So Tamar stayed on, desolate, in her brother Absalom's house.
When King David heard the whole story, he became very angry.
Absalom never said a word to Amnon, good or bad, though he hated him deeply for violating his sister Tamar.
Two full years later, Absalom held a sheep-shearing at Baal-hazor near Ephraim, and he invited all the king's sons.
Absalom came to the king and said, "Your servant is having his sheep sheared; would the king and his officials come along with your servant?"
The king answered, "No, my son, we shouldn't all go — it would be too much of a burden on you." Absalom kept pressing, but David wouldn't go, though he gave him his blessing.
Absalom said, "If not, then please let my brother Amnon come with us." The king asked, "Why should he go with you?"
But Absalom kept pressing until David let Amnon and all his other sons go along.

Absalom instructed his servants: "Watch for the moment Amnon is merry with wine, and when I give the word to strike him, kill him. Don't be afraid — I'm the one giving this order. Be strong and brave about it."
Absalom's servants carried out his order against Amnon exactly as told; then all the other sons of the king jumped on their mules and fled.
While they were still on the road, word reached David that Absalom had killed every one of the king's sons, not one left.
The king got up, tore his clothes, and lay down on the ground; all his attendants standing near him tore their clothes too.

But Jonadab, son of David's brother Shimeah, spoke up: "Don't let my lord think they killed all the young men, the king's sons — only Amnon is dead. Absalom has had this planned ever since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar."
"So don't let my lord the king take it to heart as if all his sons were dead — only Amnon is dead."
Meanwhile Absalom fled. The lookout on watch glanced up and saw a large group coming down the road from the hillside behind him.
Jonadab told the king, "Look, the king's sons are arriving — it's just as your servant said."
As soon as he finished saying it, the king's sons arrived, weeping loudly, and the king and all his servants wept bitterly along with them.
Absalom, however, had fled to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. David mourned for his son every day.
So Absalom, having fled to Geshur, stayed there three years.
And in time King David's heart stopped grieving and began to long for Absalom, now that he was consoled over Amnon's death.
